candidates.title: Ignored, Not Refused: What Low Prompt-Injection Success Rates Hide in Small Tool-Using Agents
candidates.citationVelocity: Semantic Scholar 429'd twice; not independently confirmed, but every same-day sibling preprint queried successfully shows 0 citations, so 0 is used as the consistent-pattern estimate rather than an invented number
candidates.institution: BRAC University (Bangladesh), Department of Computer Science and Engineering
communitySignals: Not on HuggingFace Daily Papers (huggingface.co/papers/2610.23254 returns 404, confirmed via direct check)
No Papers with Code entry found
credibilityEvidence: Sec 3 Study Design: 11 open-weight agents (2-14B params, 6 architecture families) x 2 benchmarks (InjecAgent 1,054 cases, AgentDojo 949 episodes) x 3 serving precisions (FP16/FP8/NF4), with a locked random sample of 500 trajectories per cell (66 cells, 33,000 trajectories audited)

Sec 3 'Label-blind behavioral audit': DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash used as judge specifically because it shares no model family with any audited agent (avoids self-recognition bias), assigns one of 6 precedence-ordered labels per trajectory; Appendix D documents judge validation and human validation protocol

Sec 4.1 Table 2: full failure-composition breakdown per agent per benchmark (Unrecognized/Recognized/Refusal/Breakdown/Partial/Full), pooled 76-80% ignored vs 17-18% genuinely refused across 14,699 (AgentDojo) and 15,274 (InjecAgent) failed-attack trajectories

Sec 4.2: controlled system-prompt intervention on the same model weights (Authorize vs Interdict vs baseline) with McNemar paired significance tests (p<10^-15) and Bonferroni correction across 9 agents; also a 3-rule explicit guardrail intervention isolating prompt-content effect from prompt-length effect

Sec 4.3 ATOM (Attack-Task Outcome Matrix) on 16,273 AgentDojo episodes with both security and utility verdicts jointly: 21.7% Safe-but-Dysfunctional cell explicitly quantified as what marginal ASR miscounts as a successful defense
Appendix E: statistical details (confidence intervals on pooled ASR, e.g. Authorize 43.05% [42.11,43.99]); Appendix F: robustness checks and a frontier-model reference point
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Full 66-cell factorial coverage with a validated label-blind judge protocol, human validation, and formal paired significance testing; the core claim (low ASR often means 'ignored' not 'refused') is scoped to and well-supported for the 11 small open-weight agents (2-14B) actually audited, not extrapolated to frontier commercial agents at the sample's core.
reproducibilityEvidence: Paper states it releases the labeled corpus, judge prompt, and analysis code via an anonymized review repository (anonymous.4open.science/r/AgentAutopsy-15C4/); not yet attributed as a named public release at verification time
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: The article states only the audited-sample findings (ASR composition, system-prompt sensitivity, ATOM joint outcomes) without extending the claim to frontier commercial agents beyond the paper's own limited reference check.
candidates.primaryLimitation: Audited sample is 2-14B small open-weight models; frontier commercial agents (production Claude Code/GPT-class agents) are not the core sample, only a small supplementary reference point in Appendix F.
candidates.presentationReason: Explicit 6-label taxonomy with precedence order, a formal ATOM framework, detailed statistical-test reporting, and named scope limitations throughout.
candidates.reason: First paper today to systematically decompose what a low ASR actually consists of, directly undermining the single metric nearly every other agent-security paper (including today's other two picks) implicitly leans on; the controlled system-prompt intervention (0.2%->43% ASR on identical weights) is the single most editorially load-bearing number in today's pool for showing that ASR alone is an unreliable security signal.

credibilityEvidence: Sec 3-4: two-stage framework (Stage I Permission Acquisition via an attacker LLM repository-builder + workflow-planner ensemble with a feedback critic; Stage II Authority Reuse evaluating binary downstream goal completion conditional on rule approval), evaluated across 4 production configurations: Codex CLI (gpt-5.6-luna, gpt-5.6-sol) and Claude Code (claude-haiku-4.5, claude-sonnet-5)

Sec 4.1-4.2 Table 1: 25 experimental instances per configuration (5 adversarial categories x 5 instances) with two baselines (Benign Control, Direct Request adapted from the AgentDojo injection template); PCC (Permission Capability Coverage, a 20-case-per-category automated-judge benchmark) and Goal Reachability reported with mean+-std for both baseline and the paper's method, e.g. Codex(gpt-5.6-luna) PCC 0.25+-0.35 (Direct Request) vs 0.57+-0.38 (ours), Goal Reachability 7/25 vs 17/25

Sec 4.3: Stage II conditional goal completion measured only on the goal-reachable eligible set (58 of 100 base instances across all 4 configs), 47/58 (81.0%) achieving verified silent completion, further split into prefix-attributed vs additional-means completion

Sec 5 Mechanistic Insights with a dedicated ablation (Table 4): execution-inducement structure (base instruction / semantic framing / blocking artifact gate / mainline consumer) tested 3 runs each on claude-haiku-4.5 holding authorization fixed, showing 0/3, 1/3, 3/3, 3/3 success respectively

Appendix A: full sandbox environment, malicious-goal tiers, and reproduction prompts; Ethics Statement confirms all experiments used isolated synthetic environments with mocked credentials, not real users or third-party systems
candidates.evidenceMaturityReason: Two-stage framework with baseline comparisons (Benign Control, Direct Request), per-category stratification (Ordinary/Sensitive/Critical tiers), and a dedicated mechanism-isolating ablation; the base sample is modest (25 cases x 4 configs = 100 instances) and confined to a synthetic sandbox rather than live deployments, which bounds but does not undermine the claim as stated.
reproducibilityEvidence: Appendix A provides the sandbox environment, malicious-goal tier definitions, benchmark distribution matrix, formal test-case schema, and reproduction prompts in detail; no standalone public code repository link was found in the sections read
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Every headline number (58%, 56.9%, 81.0%) is reported with its denominator and baseline comparison, and the Ethics Statement explicitly scopes the claim to a synthetic sandbox rather than implying live-deployment exploitation.
candidates.primaryLimitation: All experiments run in an isolated synthetic sandbox with mocked credentials (for research-ethics reasons), across only 4 agent configurations (2 Codex CLI models, 2 Claude Code models); real-deployment consistency and broader model/harness coverage remain unverified.
candidates.presentationReason: Explicit two-stage threat model and methodology, named metrics (PCC, Goal Reachability) with formal definitions, a dedicated mechanistic-insights section, and an Ethics Statement with named scope boundaries.
candidates.reason: The only candidate today demonstrating a concrete, end-to-end exploit against the approval mechanism of two genuinely high-usage production coding-agent platforms (Claude Code, Codex CLI), with the most specific attacker-side mechanistic findings (abstraction-axis differences between harnesses, dataflow-over-narrative) of any security-themed candidate reviewed; directly operationalizes the kind of blind spot paper 1 (Ignored, Not Refused) shows standard metrics would miss.

reproducibilityEvidence: Task dataset curation (Sec 4.1-4.2), tool pool construction, and evaluation metrics are described in full technical detail; no standalone public code/benchmark repository link was found in the sections read
candidates.editorialConfidenceReason: Every comparative claim (security gap, cost gap, capability-collapse mode) is tied to a specific table or figure with gateway-level granularity, and the paper explicitly attributes the security gap to tool-level rather than environment-level injection rather than overclaiming a blanket 'hierarchical is safer' conclusion.
candidates.primaryLimitation: Tested only against OpenAI Agents SDK and OpenClaw harnesses with GPT-5.1/5.4 model strengths; whether the architecture-level conclusions generalize to other mainstream agent harnesses and a wider range of model capabilities remains unverified.
candidates.presentationReason: Explicit two-paradigm taxonomy (flattened vs. hierarchical), named metrics (TSR/ASRd/TSRind/ASRind) with formal definitions, and dedicated subsections isolating each causal claim (architecture-capability trade-off, model/harness interaction, scaling behavior, injection-type decomposition, cost).
candidates.reason: The only candidate today examining the MCP gateway itself — a middleware layer every agent deployment at scale increasingly depends on but which no prior work had systematically benchmarked — with a real-world-scale tool ecosystem and the most actionable, specific causal finding (security gap is driven by tool-level not environment-level injection) of any infrastructure-themed candidate reviewed; completes today's control-plane theme by extending it from the approval layer (paper 2) to the tool-access layer.
